title: The Social Psychology of Compassion
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: Reizan Bob Penny takes up Numbers and Nerves, the book by Paul and Scott Slovic, and its research on why people stop responding to suffering at large scale. Starting from the wildfires in Oregon and the burning of Lahaina, Reizan describes Paul's findings: psychophysical numbing, shown with candles lit in a dark room, then compassion fade, the drowning-child question, and the prominence effect. Reizan closes with Annie Dillard's instruction to multiply yourself by 1,198,500,000 and Zbigniew Herbert's poem "Mr. Cogito Reads the Newspaper." In the discussion, Reizan answers questions on hope and numbness by describing sitting practice as staying alive to sensation, and the great vows as "just one more step in that direction."

I'm really sorry, I can't be there.
I was fully intending on being there, and I was excited because I haven't been in person with you guys in a long time.
But I was hanging out with somebody last night, and this morning they tested positive for COVID.
So I thought, okay, I can isolate a little bit.
Otherwise, I would be sorry.
We also had to cancel a little walk we had tonight.
It was one of our hikes, our newest little addition to our hike program, which I've called the Cedarwood Pilgrimage.
This is going to be something we're going to try and do every year, because tomorrow, this weekend, begins our mountains and rivers backpacking retreat.
The Cedarwood Pilgrimage starts at the salt water at the mouth of Little Squalicum Creek, and it goes up that canyon right to our new Dharma Hall at Cedarwood.
We would also go up to Cornwall Park.
So we'd go up from the salt water to Cornwall Park, where there's some flat bedrock that the creek goes over right there in the park.
That was the crossing point for the old [unclear: "Metzach"] trail, and also where the original telegraph road crossed.
They would cross wagons across [unclear: "that good Rocks that they could"], the shallow area that had a firm underpinning where they could ford the creek.
So the idea with that walk is that we'd be beginning our hike to the mountain, beginning our journey to the mountain, maybe with community members.
It's always been our idea that the community sends us, the seekers, off to the wilderness.
We didn't get to do that, but we will start doing that next year, I hope.
We do end up doing the retreat.
We begin the retreat at my farm, a little farther up the drainage of the watershed, starting at home.
The idea is to remove that notion that you blast off to those recreational areas that are way up there.
We live here; that's up there.
We come to it from the grounding space of home as we travel into the mountains.
We spend time at the farm, out in our cedar grove, doing intention-setting ceremonies so that every member gets to speak about their thoughts about the journey.
The hikers will be going to the mountain, our mountain, which is the source of our waters, where the mountains make the clouds rise to drop the waters onto our land.
And we return changed, renewed, maybe ready to extend ourselves to others.
It's a connection to all of our heights, in that we're following the way of the water, is what we call it.
We pick up a little vial of Salish seawater in March.

We divide it into three vials, and then on these journeys, like on this backpack, we go to the far upper reaches of each of the three watersheds of the Nooksack and we exchange those vials for mountain water.
At the end of the season, we bring that all back down to the place where we got the water at the beginning of the season and return it to the Salish Sea.
So we do this journey with life-giving water to stay attentive, aware and feeling for our place and the changes in nature in our new age of rapid warming.
But as a society, I feel we most often largely stay within the narrow awareness bubble.
[unclear: "If gauge for our feeling response."] And a cursory look shows us to be nearly asleep to our likely fate.
To the south, our neighbors in Oregon are going through their feelings all over again.
They came to my aunt's hometown of Blue River, as well as Vida and McKenzie Bridge, as well as the [unclear: "San Diego River"], the beloved home of noted naturalist and author Barry Lopez.
All of it went to flames a couple of years ago.
Lopez had evacuated in that event and was not in good health at the time, and died without, perhaps thankfully, ever seeing that destruction of what he had written about and loved for so many years.
Fire is there again as we speak.
The towns are evacuated again.
This week, one morning, Eugenians awoke to ash on their windows and cars. 103 degrees Celsius.
The smoke-filled air and blood-red sun, over a red flag warning and preliminary evacuation preparations.
My childhood summer camp, sparkling little Fall Creek.
Just think of the North Fork here and our precious sacred old grove up there and Glacier and Maple Falls and Kendall, all gone.
It's a beautiful place to be. [unclear: "Where the crowd is startled through forested ponds is on fire."]

And of course, one could also mention Maui and Yellowknife or any of the other tragedies of recent years: the hurricanes, heat domes, floods, atmospheric rivers, wet blobs, fire tornadoes, bomb cyclones.

We keep reaching for descriptors to make sense of things, to find responsiveness to things like 102-degree oceans in Florida, or [unclear: "the single dumping of rain in the day, which was an annual not as it seems made this weekend before the Southwest"].
So much of this information is conveyed to us in what we've become accustomed to as the blithering array of numbers.
Numbers greater and greater, and yet producing still far too low a response.
We exist numb, in a psychic state of disbelief that any of this will happen to us.
Or if we conjure the imagination that it may happen to us, we still don't connect with the feelings.
We still don't connect with the feelings, the feeling of sheer terror that infected the people of Lahaina as they ran for their lives and dove into the ocean to save themselves.
And yet we all stand at the edge of that same ocean, that precipice, with little room left to move.
Instead, we read the news in our news-obsessed brains, like prurient voyeurs, titillated, perhaps excited, just enough but not too much.
Excited, though, and yet burned out on the images and information, the numbers.
We turn to distraction, to entertainment, and feel our duty has been done because we are now informed.
Noting how this all goes, we here have been choosing instead to take time from our distractions and follow the way of water.
We keep ourselves awake, aware, feeling for, present, ready.

This is why we do these practices in place: not to use nature as a storehouse of peace from which to withdraw our suffering, but instead as the great community of needful beings and habitations requiring our compassionate response, our joyful participation.
Our work is to awaken our compassionate response, because compassion has no function except in active response.
We know the image of Avalokiteshvara with countless arms, each holding [unclear: "for"] yet another tool, a tool of upaya, of skillful means, a myriad and endless plethora of compassionate responses.
This is our inspiration.
And yet, I think we can all admit that we as a society are not responding.
We are instead reeling in shock and distracting ourselves with the mundane usualness of our activity-filled lives.

I've told people I know for years now that the time needs to come, needs to come much sooner than it is coming, where our position towards what has already become the continuous whirlwind of disasters in the world moves firmly away from crisis response and instead becomes ever-present, engaged compassion in action.
It's clear this is not happening, not anywhere in the scale and speed to measure it [unclear: "with danger"].
We, who are special practitioners of compassion, need to understand the dynamics of this society's and humans' numb to responses and to provide antidotes.
I'm thinking a lot about Hawaii this week because I was born there.
One of my closest friends is exactly my same age.
We share a birthday.
We came into the world on exactly the same day.
Crosstown rivals in junior high track and field, by our senior year of high school we were co-team captains.
Scott Slovak was always a serious and extremely studious partner to my artistic and expressive nature.
But we at core had very similar concerns in this world.
Scott has become perhaps one of the best known critical thinkers today by examining American nature writing.
Most soft-spoken and exact in speech, Scott and his father Paul always seemed of one mind.
Paul's [unclear: "new"] group of runners has for over 50 years jogged along the streets of Eugene.

It was there on those Eugene runs, and at Sun River with Paul's cadre of running social psychologist statisticians, where Paul and Scott fell into collaborative discussions exploring the question of why the famine and genocide in Darfur could not get resolved.

And what insights about responsiveness of feelings could be gained by setting Paul's statistical research on human motivation alongside Scott's understanding of the efforts of artists and writers who delve into looking deeply at this world?
The result of their collaboration was this small and deeply useful book, Numbers and Nerves, Information, Emotion and Meaning in a World of Darfur.
There is much here in this book and I haven't finished reading it all.
Contributors [unclear: "stand"] from scientists presenting research findings to the musings of the likes of Terry Tempest Williams, Bill McKibben and Rick Bass.
Visual art and conceptual art is discussed, as well as political messaging and the ubiquitous train of information we receive from the media.
In the book, a refrain they're referring to is the final line of a poem from which they had initially launched their discussions on the run.
The line: the arithmetic of compassion.
From this book, I'm choosing here to outline a few of Paul's most striking research insights to see how they may contribute to our own practice of compassionate awareness and engagement.
So, I'm going to conduct a quick experiment.
It really stings when I do that.
But if I do it steadily and repeatedly, the sting soon mitigates, dissipates, numbs and becomes normalized.
Normalizing stress is a common survival strategy of organisms.
We can see similar responses looking at food or light or warmth or many other stressors or inputs.
That's common biology.
And yet, if we normalize the type of danger we now face in this world, we will all perish like the proverbial frog boiling in a pot of water.
Paul found, from viewing an experimental film at the University of Oregon, that when one candle was lit in the darkened space, our eyes register that as a very positive introduction of light.
Two candles is more light, but not double to our perceptions, not twice what the single candle impressed us with.
And when 20 candles are lit, the introduction of a 21st brings almost zero responsiveness from us.
These phenomena, which are statistically repeatable in many different sorts of experiments, he termed psychophysical numbing.
These results were [unclear: "encountered"] to intuitive thinking.
In the [unclear: "rocketedly"] named chapter, the more who die, the less we care, graphs are shown.
In the first, the line, we assume that each life is equal and worth.
Anyone would objectively agree with that.
And so we imagine a graph of loss versus value to be a straight slope upwards when it comes to tragic loss.
Each life lost would raise our sense of the tragedy incrementally upward in a straight line, in equal steps for each life lost.
And additionally, one could also assume another intuitive deduction: that perhaps the volume of deaths itself is a tragedy.
Such that one lost life is valued in some way, but when multiple lives are lost, it adds up to greater than the sum of its parts.
The curve sweeping upward somewhat because more loss is so tragic.
But despite these notions, research figures out that two other graphs are more true to how we respond to the world.
In the next graph, the curve goes up, but then gently curves downward as more and more lives are lost, at some point [unclear: "lavelling"] off.
Our ability to be as hurt, as distraught, as concerned with many lives lost is not the sum of the number of lives.
We lose the ability to care as the number increases.
Like just getting slapped on the arm several more times.
Whose counting seems to be our effective response.
This was termed compassion fade.
And then another graph emerged from the research.
This graph goes up like the other curves, to flatten out and then tumbles down to a low level.
This is where we've heard enough.
We turn off the news.
We don't want to get any more involved.
This is called compassion collapse.
When a question was asked, given even that there's some inherent risk to you, if you saw a child drowning just offshore and you could save him, would you?
If you saw a child drowning just offshore and you could save him, would you?
But when the idea of a second child was brought into the scenario, a child farther offshore, one you could not save, would you still save the one you could?
Surprisingly, the answer, the yes answer, is reduced by nearly half.
Introducing up to six children you could not save did not change that number much.
The damage to motivation had occurred with just one child who could not be saved.

Psychic numbing, a diminished capacity or inclination to feel, was joined by a phenomenon they called [unclear: "pseudo in efficacy"]: the notion that since you can't save them all, then what's the point?
But even when we believe that we feel and care about people in the world, why do we keep making choices that don't reflect that?
Here I'm thinking especially about society and politics, but we can see this somewhere inside our own lives too. [unclear: "Paul deduced"] something he called the prominence effect.
When something is in our choice matrix and we feel it's an absolute given or necessity, then the other choices available, no matter what they are, are never chosen.
It doesn't matter even if we objectively believe that we understand the choices to be of some sort of equal value.
When research subjects were offered a choice between cash money and an equal value of store coupons, I bet you can guess which they almost always chose.
Cash has a prominence effect in that equation, as does national security in almost every decision we make as a country to address famine, genocide or the climate crisis.
The prominence effect will continue to trump all other choices until we somehow rewire our perceptions of risk.
How this operates for each of us at the personal level is an important question for us to keep in mind as practitioners of compassion.
How can we apply these insights to our practice?
For one, knowledge seems to be very helpful.
In research, it was found that simply unpacking for the research subjects the notions behind these various concepts [unclear: "of that line"] could almost wholly dissipate these statistical effects.
If we are wise to our own games, we see right through them.
Subjects did the experiments and confirmed they responded as most do in accord with these effects.
Then they were educated about them and scored much differently on a second round, almost statistically nil between the choices offered.
This didn't work in all cases, though, and the prominence effect seemed a particularly sticky one to unhook from.
But researchers also found that there were some subjects who never seemed to make choices in line with these effects.
They seemed to have compassion and response engaged already and sailed through the questions.
They saved the child, gave the money away, cured the famine or whatever it was, and in each case responded in a manner we might hope for.
What was up with these people?
Well, it seems when asked that they were using a different arithmetic of compassion.
As one author quoted in the book says about the Holocaust, it was not six million murders.
It was one murder six million times.
Or, as writer Annie Dillard says in the frontispiece quotation:
*There are 1,198,500,000 people alive in China.
To get a feel for what this means, simply take yourself, in all your singularity, importance, complexity, and love, and multiply it by 1,198,500,000.
See?
Nothing to it.*
There's much more in this book.
I plan to finish it and study it with some intensity.
My good friends Scott and Paul have really come up with something here.
I recommend this book because I feel it reaches into many and various issues and approaches and can be utilized widely by artists, politicians, and practitioners.
I believe they made it small and accessible for just that reason.
I'll finish here with the poem that started them on their journey of inquiry, [unclear: "The big new Herbert's"] Mr.
Cogito Reads the Newspaper.
If you pay attention, it mentions all sorts of quantification but is vague about actual numbers.
Or when numbers are given, it makes them whole numbers, ending in zeros, therefore abstract.
It says "described with precision," but nothing in this gives much particular description to differentiate all this from the common tragedies repeated every day of our lives.
And that seems to be the poem's point.
So, Mr.
Cogito Reads the Newspaper by [unclear: "Zimmerer Herbert"].
*On the first page, a report of the killing of 120 soldiers.
The war lasted a long time.
You could get used to it.*
*Close alongside the news of the sensational crime was a portrait of the murderer.
The eye of Mr.
Cogito slips indifferently over the soldiers' hecatomb to plunge with delight into the description of everyday horrors.
A 30-year-old farm laborer, under the stress of nervous depression, killed his wife and two small children.
It is described with precision, the course of the murder, the position of the bodies, and other details.
For 120 dead, you search on a map in vain.
Too great a distance covers them like a jungle.
They don't speak to the imagination.
There are too many of them.*
*The numerical zero at the end changes them into an abstraction.
A subject for meditation.
The arithmetic of compassion.*
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Thank you.
I wanted to keep it a little short because I thought this would bring up a few questions.
So rather than trying to answer things myself, I thought I'd let you ask questions and see what you came up with in this.

**Participant:** Bob, I'm not in the room.
I'm on camera.

When you were talking about Lahaina, I know someone who lost friends there, who perished in the fire, and mentioned that there were also people slumped over the wall that they couldn't get over that had died on that wall because they were trying to get to the water, but they were either physically challenged or mentally challenged and they couldn't make it, and there they hung on the wall.
So it just makes me stop and think of how it's all around us so much, and I don't mean to dwell on it, but just to remember that it is there,
**Participant:** And so that's what I thought about when you were talking.
Thank you.
I really appreciate your talk, and I'm probably going to go out and get that book, but I'm wondering if you could say more about the role of practice in working with this numbness.
In what ways do you see Zen teachings and Zen practice sort of being an antidote, if you want to call it that, for this numbness?
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Well, I think the heart of our practice is to stay present and aware, and in that sense we are engaged with feeling, engaged with sensation.
So at a very core level our practice helps us understand feeling and sensation and be sensitive to it, be really aware of it at a heightened level.
That's just sort of baked into our practice deeply, and I think that's why in our Mahayana tradition compassion is so emphasized, because that's what you see when you look inside.
You see that you feel and you are connected to others, so compassion naturally is part of that, it rises out of that.
I always feel like Zen people are fairly brave, and it's going to take bravery to meet this future because the practice isn't easy.
We do it anyway because we just feel that there's something there.
The difficulty doesn't matter, we're willing to do it.
All of those qualities, I think, are good, and I think the insights in the book are things we might be able to cycle back into our actual personal moment-by-moment practice.

How do we find ourselves numbing out to things, distracting ourselves, or devaluing situations, because we are just sort of seeing them, noticing that we're seeing them devalued because we're subjected to them too much or something?

It's important, and it was hopeful for me in the book to note that people generally can radically change their choices and actions just by understanding those particular natural responses that we have, that we just sort of operate on.
So I'm excited to learn more about that and just see how it filters back into a grounded sitting practice, and just find more applications and insights for those insights.
**Participant:** Thank you.
I was thinking that one of the reasons people get sort of overwhelmed by the numbers is just the thought that this is so overwhelming that there's no way I can do anything to change it.
And I think that Zen practice uniquely helps with that, because I've never met anyone who just sat down once and [unclear: "stood up a night"], and yet we do it over and over and over again.
And every time, we're going to finish this dharma talk with a pledge to save all beings that we know we'll never fulfill.
And so each of us needs to make, if all of us just keep working at it, it will make a difference.
And I think that's for me where practice comes into this: I can't cure this problem, but I can help.
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Yeah, exactly.

Having a sense that it's an impossible task, but willingly accepting that impossible task, like the great vows, is really the heart of that kind of approach, because life is sort of an impossible task.
So you could just curl up and roll away, or you could try and live your life.
And you'll fail, you'll fail, but all along there's the sweetness and the successes.
It doesn't happen without the effort, right?
So there's always something, there's always sort of a spear point, meaning a pointed edge, a point of engagement of our practice.
We're working something all the time.
We've got something we can be doing, either it's a kindness to ourselves or a kindness to others, or a compassionate response.
It's not everything.
We're not going to save the world, but we always have this thing we can keep doing.
We're always able to be moving one more step in that direction.
And that's really the practice, just one more step in that direction.
**Participant:** Bob, can you hear me?
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Yeah.
Hey, Scott.
**Participant:** Hi.
Nice to see you, my friend.
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Good to see you too.

**Participant:** Along with what Ken was talking about, we're always inundated with negativism and fear, and just a whole bunch of tactics to basically keep us either scared or inflamed, and keep us watching the TV set, among other things.
Can you comment a little bit more on how, I think that to a certain extent my Zen practice is a good antidote to a lot of that, not all of it.
But at least I don't think, with the practice, I don't think we get that cumulative numbing that you were talking about when you were slapping your wrist.
Can you comment on that a little bit?
**Reizan Bob Penny:** Well, that's interesting.
Yeah.
Our practice doesn't seem to numb us out, even though it's repetitive, and static, and all these kinds of things.
Maybe this is really what has always been said about our practice, and the way Dogen emphasized it: it's miraculous.
It's got like no moving parts.
There's nothing to it.
You don't have to be smart, or dumb, or whatever.
And it's open and free for all.
So there's something about the process of being an open door to our experience, an open door to sensation, that is constantly enlightening me.
And I think it has something to do with that sensation level.
I remember in my very first meditation retreat, which I did in that Sri Lanka tradition, the idea was the 12-step chain of causation, if you're familiar with that, and the origination.
The level of sensation, which is before perception, was the entry point on the meditative path: to [unclear: "feel the growth"], to feel the sensation of it in the moment.
To be alive with feeling before thought was the place to intercede with the chain of events, the chain of cycles of stories in our brains, and the cycle of karma in our lives.
So it's interesting that that coincides with what's talked about in this book about nerves or affected feelings, as opposed to numbers.
So I think we're on the right track with our practice.
We're working at the core level of sensation.
We're staying alive to this.
Thank you, Bob.
Bob, I've got a question for you, or a thought.
First, thank you for alerting us to this material and this perspective on our world and ourselves.
I thought about the numbing process, and first of all, I think it's self-protection, right?
But as long as I think about the "else," I can sit back and watch it.
We're taught that it's not us and them.
We're all together, and if I can think that I am that person hanging on the wall, I am the firefighter that got engulfed in the planes, it brings it alive.
And then we have our practice that says, be with this, no matter how awful it feels, be with it, and then somehow we find a way into action.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
That sounds beautiful.
I think that we, as a group, as a whole, Zen people are probably basically engaged in compassionate work.
Just the sitting itself is that engagement, but also just their lives in general, because it's coming out of that.
So hopefully we're working, [unclear: "we're not known"], but there might be ways in which we are that we aren't noticing, so it's always good to think about that and wonder what we're missing there.
I find some of these insights intriguing.
They bring up questions for me about how that is for me.
But there's nothing like the real thing.

I think journalism has figured out that, for instance, one of the things in the book was, and I think a lot of the aid agencies in African places like that have figured this out: if you show the picture of just one person and say, can you help this child, they get way more donations than if they show a picture of one person and say, there are millions of kids like Susie, can you contribute to help them.
You get far fewer contributions that way.

So we're hardwired to respond to each other individually and to be motivated by seeing ourselves in their shoes, like, imagine what if that was you in Lahaina or whatever, where journalism shows first-person accounts and you hear it from them.
I know in 2005, when my son was 13, he had to do a bar mitzvah service project, so I took him to Biloxi, Mississippi, after Katrina, and we spent a week [unclear: "doing an Easter"].
It was definitely a drop in the bucket in terms of what needed to happen down there, to think that you were making any difference.
But I saw it firsthand, in a way you never would see it.
I understood it in a whole different way, because I got it from their shoes, so to speak.
So we need that.

And I've noticed that things like the wildfires down in Oregon that are much more prevalent [unclear: "that really appear in Bellingham"], because, well, maybe there'll be a fire, we're not really realizing how on the edge we are.
I know places down there where it's happened and it's bad, and it's not that far away.

So to connect with places where it's happening, to connect with people, to understand what's really happening, I think it's becoming, my sense about it is that we're going to make a turning as a society, and I think it's about to happen.
It's going to happen with the increase of these disasters.

You get a year like this, and continuing next year, now this is a constant drumbeat in the information system, that things are happening around the planet, big energy systems are moving, everybody's becoming more aware and educated about it.
So this is all an expression of attention and awareness, not numbing, not numbing out, so maybe we're waking up somewhat.
I'm hopeful for that.

Yeah.

verbatim.text: Okay, all right. I'm really sorry, I can't be there. I was fully intending on being there. And I was excited because I haven't been in person with you guys in a long time, but I was hanging out with somebody last night. And this morning, they tested positive for COVID. So I thought, okay, I can isolate a little bit. So otherwise, I would be sorry. We also had to cancel a little walk we had tonight. One of our hikes, our newest little addition to our hike program, which I've called the Cedarwood Pilgrimage. And this is going to be something we're going to try and do every year. Because tomorrow, this weekend begins our mountains and rivers backpacking retreat. And so the Cedarwood Pilgrimage starts at the salt water at the mouth of Little Squalicum Creek, and it goes up that canyon, and it goes right to our, our new Dharma Hall and Cedarwood. And we would also go up to Cornwall Park. So we'd go up in the salt water up to Cornwall Park, where there's some flat bedrock that the creek goes over right there in the park. That was the crossing point for the old Metzach trail and also where the original telegraph road, they would cross wagons across that good Rocks that they could, the shallow area that we had a firm underpinning that they could forward the creek here. So the idea with that walk is that we'd be sort of beginning our hike to the mountain, beginning our journey to the mountain, maybe with community members. And that's been always been our ideas that the community sends us off to the wilderness to the seekers. So we didn't get to do that, but we will start doing that next year, I hope. And we, we end up doing the retreat. We begin the retreat at my farm a little farther up the drainage of the watershed, starting at home. The idea is to

Kind of remove that notion that you blast off to those recreational areas that are way up there. We live here, that's up there. We come to it from the grounding space from home as we travel into the mountains. And we spend time at the farm out in our Cedar Grove doing an intention setting. Ceremonies so that every member gets to speak about their, their thoughts about the journey. The hikers will be going to the mountain, the mountain, our mountain, which is the source of our waters. Where the mountains make the clouds rise to drop the waters onto our land and And we return, changed, renewed, maybe ready to extend ourselves to others.
